# The Evil Hypnotist (Part 2/5)

## A Story of Compulsion and Control

---

NAME_1 stood frozen at the edge of the stage, his sneakers planted on the worn wooden boards, the hot white spotlights beating down on him from above. The audience was a dark mass of faces beyond the glare, maybe two hundred people seated in the old converted theater, and every single one of them was looking at him. He could feel the weight of their collective attention like a physical thing pressing against his chest.

He was sixteen years old, and he had absolutely no idea why he was here.

That was the thing that kept nagging at him, threading through his confusion like a splinter working its way under skin. He remembered the week leading up to tonight with perfect clarity — he remembered thinking about the show, sure, but only in the vague way you thought about things that had already happened. He hadn't planned to come back. He hadn't bought a ticket. He hadn't told his parents he was going out, exactly — he'd said he was going to Marcus's house, which was a lie, and he felt bad about that, but at the time it had seemed like the natural thing to say.

The natural thing. That was rich.

Nothing about tonight was natural.

He'd gotten dressed around seven o'clock, pulling on his good jeans and a clean shirt without really thinking about why, eaten dinner with his family, laughed at something his little sister said, and then at seven forty-five had simply walked out the front door and taken three buses across town to this theater. The Meridian Theater, according to the marquee outside, a faded art deco building sandwiched between a Vietnamese restaurant and a cell phone repair shop on the kind of street that got quieter after dark.

The sign outside had read: **NAME_2 — MASTER OF MINDS — ADULT SHOW — 18+ STRICTLY ENFORCED.**

He'd walked straight past the sign without reading it, or rather — he'd read it but the words hadn't seemed to apply to him. There had been a man at the door, heavyset, with the bored expression of someone who'd spent too many years doing this job, and NAME_1 had expected to be turned away. He'd half-hoped to be turned away, actually, because that would have given him an excuse to go home and the whole strange compulsion would have resolved itself.

But the man had looked at him, and something had shifted in his eyes — a flicker of recognition, almost — and he'd simply unhooked the velvet rope and let him through without a word.

That had been strange. That had been the first thing that had crept under NAME_1's skin and made him feel genuinely uneasy.

He'd found a seat near the back of the theater, in the section that was maybe a third full at that point, surrounded by adults who'd glanced at him curiously and then looked away. The seats were plush and old, the kind that creaked when you shifted your weight. The ceiling was decorated with painted plaster that had seen better days, cherubs and clouds and theatrical masks peering down through flaking gilt paint.

He'd sat there for twenty minutes while the theater filled up around him, trying to figure out why he'd come.

*I just wanted to see the show again,* he'd thought. *The first show was funny. This will be funny too.*

But that wasn't quite right, and he knew it. He hadn't wanted to see the show. There had been no wanting involved, not really. It was more like — like how you didn't *want* to breathe, exactly. You just did it. You didn't make a choice about it. It happened.

He'd been breathing his way across town to this theater all evening, and now he was standing on the stage under the lights, and NAME_2 was looking at him with those dark, amused eyes, and he still couldn't quite make himself feel properly alarmed about any of it.

---

NAME_2 was not what you'd expect a stage hypnotist to look like, if your expectations had been formed by old movies or daytime television. She was perhaps thirty-five, or perhaps ten years older than that — it was genuinely difficult to tell. She was tall, dressed in a deep burgundy suit that fit her with the precision of something custom-made, her dark hair pulled back from her face in a way that emphasized the sharp geometry of her cheekbones. She wore very little jewelry — just small earrings and a single ring on her right hand, silver, with a flat black stone set in it.

She had the kind of presence that made a room feel smaller when she was in it. Not threatening, exactly — not immediately threatening — but *concentrated*, like the air around her was denser somehow, like she occupied more space than her physical dimensions should have allowed.

Her assistant, NAME_3, was a contrast in almost every way. She was younger, maybe mid-twenties, with a bright open smile and warm brown skin and natural hair pulled up in a loose bun. She wore a simple black dress and moved with the easy confidence of someone comfortable in their body. She was pretty and approachable and her job, NAME_1 was beginning to suspect, was partly to make the audience feel safe, to soften the edge of whatever NAME_2 was actually doing.

When NAME_4 had said his name — *"Ladies and Gentlemen, let me introduce today's volunteer, NAME_1!"* — his body had moved before his mind had caught up. He'd stood up from his seat at the back of the theater and walked down the central aisle toward the stage with the calm, steady purpose of a person who had been asked to do something completely ordinary and was simply doing it.

He hadn't decided to stand up. He hadn't decided to walk down the aisle.

But he had done both of those things, and his body had felt perfectly relaxed while doing them, and it was only somewhere in the back of his mind that a small, increasingly frantic voice was asking what the hell was happening.

NAME_5 had been waiting at the side of the stage. She'd extended her hand to help him up the steps — a small, courteous gesture — and her grip had been warm and firm, and she'd smiled at him with that open, friendly smile, and something about the normalcy of it had quieted the voice in the back of his mind almost immediately.

*See,* the voice said, somewhat mollified. *She's nice. This is fine. This is a show.*

Now he stood beside NAME_4 at the center of the stage, facing the audience, the lights warm on his face, and NAME_4 was looking at him with an expression he couldn't quite read. There was satisfaction in it, definitely. There was something that might have been anticipation. And there was something else, something cooler and more calculating, that she kept mostly hidden behind the warmth of her stage persona.

"Normally," NAME_4 said, turning back to address the audience, her voice carrying perfectly in the old theater's acoustics, "we would now hypnotize our volunteer at this point in time. But with NAME_1, that is hardly necessary." She paused, letting the statement settle over the audience. "Let me prove it to you."

She turned back to him, and her eyes met his, and she said, calmly and quietly, almost conversationally: "NAME_1. Stand completely still."

---

He stood completely still.

This was not unusual. He'd already been standing still. But there was a difference between standing still because you were choosing to and standing still because — because the option of not standing still had simply ceased to exist. It was like being a photograph of yourself. The idea of moving was still present in his mind, fully formed, but the connection between the idea and his muscles had been gently, precisely severed.

The audience responded with a murmur of appreciation.

"He came here tonight," NAME_4 said, walking slowly around him as she spoke, addressing the audience in the easy, unhurried tone of someone explaining something obvious, "because I told him to. Last week, when NAME_1 participated in my public demonstration, I took the opportunity to plant a specific post-hypnotic suggestion. A compulsion. He spent the past seven days entirely unaware of it, going about his normal teenage life —" there was a ripple of laughter from the audience at this, warm and knowing "— until this evening, when it activated, and he found himself making his way across the city to be here with us tonight."

She was speaking about him in the third person while he was standing right there, which ought to have been humiliating, but he found that he couldn't quite work up any feeling about it. Couldn't work up any feeling about much of anything, actually. He was aware of everything — the lights, the audience, NAME_4's voice, NAME_5 standing to his left watching him with professional attention — but it all felt slightly remote, like he was observing it from a small but significant distance.

"What NAME_1 is experiencing right now," NAME_4 continued, stopping in front of him and addressing the audience over his shoulder, "is a state that I call *passive compliance*. He is fully conscious. He is aware of what is happening to him. He can hear and understand everything I say." She looked at him directly. "Can't you, NAME_1?"

"Yes," he said. His voice sounded normal. That surprised him a little.

"He simply finds it very difficult to resist my instructions. The suggestion I planted last week created a pathway — a kind of open door in his mind that allows me to direct his behavior without the full induction process." She smiled at the audience. "It's considerably more efficient. And rather more interesting to watch, I think."

More laughter, more appreciative murmuring.

"Now," NAME_4 said, "let's give NAME_1 his movement back — partially — and see what he makes of his situation."

She said it casually, almost as an afterthought, but the effect was immediate. The frozen quality lifted from his muscles and he could move again, and the first thing he did was turn his head and look at NAME_4 with an expression that he suspected communicated his feelings fairly accurately.

NAME_4 looked back at him, composed and slightly amused.

"How are you feeling?" she asked.

NAME_1 thought about lying. He thought about saying *fine* in a tone that suggested the opposite, the way you did when an adult asked how you were doing and you didn't want to have a real conversation. But the question had been asked directly and sincerely, more or less, and he found that the words that came out of his mouth were the honest ones.

"Confused," he said.

"Of course you are. That's completely understandable." She gestured graciously, as though acknowledging a reasonable point in a debate. "Would you like to understand what's happening to you?"

The honest answer was yes. Absolutely yes. He wanted to understand very much.

"Yes," he said.

"Then sit down," she said, and NAME_5 was already there with a chair — a plain wooden chair positioned at the center of the stage — and he sat in it, not because he'd decided to but because his body had interpreted her instruction as something that simply needed to be done.

---

The chair was harder than it looked. He shifted slightly, trying to find a comfortable position, and found that he could do that — he had movement within certain parameters, it seemed, like an animal on a long leash. He could fidget. He could turn his head and look around. He couldn't, he suspected, stand up and walk off the stage.

He tested this theory carefully, keeping his expression neutral, trying to be subtle about it. He thought about standing. He thought about it quite clearly and specifically — the mechanics of it, the shift of weight, the pushing up from the seat. He could feel the intention forming in his mind like a plan, detailed and ready.

It just didn't go anywhere.

His legs stayed where they were. His hands stayed in his lap. He sat in the chair on the stage in front of two hundred strangers while NAME_4 paced at the edge of the stage and spoke to the audience about the architecture of suggestion, about the pathways of the unconscious mind, and he listened to her with the particular quality of attention you gave to something that was directly relevant to your situation.

"The important distinction to understand," NAME_4 was saying, "is between hypnosis as entertainment and hypnosis as a genuine modification of behavior. What most people have seen — the stage shows, the comedy routines, the daytime television demonstrations — operate on one principle: they lower resistance and invite participation. The subject cooperates because, on some level, they want to cooperate. The hypnotist facilitates an experience the subject is already disposed toward."

She paused.

"What I do is different."

The audience was very quiet.

"The suggestion I planted in NAME_1 last week was not an invitation. It was an instruction. It bypassed his preferences and his choices and his conscious decision-making entirely, and it put something into him that operated below his awareness until the moment it activated." She glanced at him. "When you got dressed to come here tonight, NAME_1, did you feel like you were making a choice?"

He thought about it honestly. "It felt like a choice," he said. "But — not quite."

"Not quite," she agreed. "It felt like choosing what to have for breakfast when you wake up already knowing what you want. The decision felt like yours, but it had already been made for you."

That was precisely right, and the precision of it was more unsettling than the thing itself.

"What I'm going to do tonight," NAME_4 said, addressing the audience again, "with NAME_1's assistance —" she said *assistance* with a very slight, very specific emphasis that made a portion of the audience laugh quietly "— is demonstrate a series of techniques that build on the foundation I established last week. Tonight's demonstration will be rather more extensive than what you saw in the family show. Which is, of course, why this is the adult show."

More laughter. NAME_1 looked out at the audience and found that he could not read their mood precisely — there was amusement there, certainly, but also something else, a quality of attention that felt more intent than the casual enjoyment of entertainment. These were people who had come specifically for this. Some of them had probably seen NAME_4 before. Some of them knew what to expect.

He didn't.

NAME_5 appeared at his shoulder, and he turned to find her crouching beside the chair, looking at him with that warm, genuinely kind expression. Up close, off to the side of the stage with the audience's attention on NAME_4, she spoke to him quietly enough that the audience couldn't hear.

"You okay?" she asked.

It was such a normal question, asked with such genuine concern, that he almost laughed.

"Not really," he said honestly.

She nodded, as though this were a perfectly reasonable answer. "It's a lot to take in," she said. "The compulsion — the feeling of not quite being in control — it can be disorienting. Especially the first time."

"The first time," he repeated.

She met his eyes steadily. "She's very careful," NAME_5 said. "I want you to know that. She doesn't do anything that causes lasting harm. Everything that happens tonight — you'll be fine afterward. I want you to believe that."

He looked at her for a moment. "Is that supposed to be reassuring?"

She smiled, a small rueful smile this time, less performed than her stage expression. "A little," she said.

"What's going to happen?" he asked.

But NAME_4's voice was rising behind them, cuing the next portion of the act, and NAME_5 straightened up and stepped back into her professional position, and the moment of private conversation ended as cleanly as a door closing.

---

"Let's begin," NAME_4 said, "with something simple. NAME_1, hold out your right hand."

He held out his right hand.

"Make a fist."

He made a fist. His fingers curled into his palm with the neat, automatic quality of a machine performing a function.

"Now open it."

He opened it.

"Now —" she paused, and the pause was theatrical but also, he was beginning to understand, functional. The pauses did something. They created a space in which the instruction that followed seemed to arrive from somewhere inside him rather than from outside. "Try to close it."

He tried to close it.

He could not close it. His hand remained open, fingers extended, perfectly flat. He applied what he was fairly certain was the maximum amount of effort and the fingers did not move. They didn't tremble with the effort. They simply stayed where they were, as relaxed and unresponsive as if the hand belonged to someone else.

The audience applauded.

"Good," NAME_4 said. "You can close your hand now."

He closed it immediately. The whole sequence had taken perhaps twenty seconds.

"What did that feel like?" she asked him.

"Like my hand wasn't mine," he said.

"In a sense, it wasn't. For those twenty seconds, it was responding to me rather than to you." She tilted her head slightly. "Does that frighten you?"

He considered the question seriously, the way you might consider a math problem you weren't sure you had the right answer to. "It should," he said.

"But does it?"

"Not as much as it should."

She smiled, and it was the first smile she'd directed at him that seemed genuinely pleased rather than performed. "That's the passive compliance at work," she said. "It smooths the emotional response. Keeps you calm. Without it, you'd be quite distressed right now, I expect."

"You're keeping me from being scared," he said slowly.

"I'm keeping you from being *paralyzed* by fear," she corrected. "There's a difference. You can still understand your situation clearly. You can still have preferences about it. You simply can't be overwhelmed by your emotional response to it." She looked at the audience. "It makes for a much more functional subject, and a much more interesting demonstration."

---

The demonstration proceeded.

Looking back on it later — in the days and weeks after that night, when he replayed the sequence of events with the obsessive, uncomfortable attention of someone trying to understand something they'd experienced but hadn't fully been present for — he found that his memories of the early part of the evening had a strange, slightly telescoped quality. Things had happened, and he had been there for all of them, but the emotional buffer NAME_4 had described kept the full weight of each moment from landing in real time.

He remembered specific things clearly.

He remembered NAME_4 making him stand and sit and stand again, like a demonstration of basic function, while she explained to the audience the mechanism of a post-hypnotic suggestion — how it differed from a real-time instruction, how the one she'd planted the previous week had been designed to survive a week of normal life without degrading or being overridden by conscious thought.

He remembered her making him hold a specific expression — a specific smile, precisely calibrated, neither too bright nor too subtle — for what she told the audience was four minutes, while she continued to talk about other things entirely, addressing the audience and occasionally walking behind him or to the side, and the smile remained precisely in place throughout as if it had been painted on.

He remembered NAME_5 bringing out a length of soft rope, and the way his stomach had tightened slightly at the sight of it, and the way NAME_4 had noticed his reaction immediately and said, "Don't worry about that yet," and the worry had smoothed itself away as though it had never been.

*Don't worry about that yet.*

He thought about those words quite a bit, afterward.

He remembered the audience laughing at things — not cruelly, but with the warm, appreciative laughter of people who were genuinely enjoying a performance — and he was aware during those moments of a complicated, layered feeling that he couldn't quite name. Not quite humiliation. Not quite the comfortable ordinariness of being the focus of friendly attention. Something between the two.

He was the subject of the show. He was the demonstration material. He was the thing being demonstrated.

He was also, the part of him that was still clearly observing noted with some discomfort, providing excellent entertainment.

---

About forty minutes into the demonstration, NAME_4 changed the pace.

She'd been building to something — he could feel it the way you could sometimes feel a shift in the weather before any visible sign of it, some atmospheric change that your body registered before your conscious mind caught up. The techniques she'd been demonstrating had been getting progressively more specific, more personal, the audience's response shifting from light amusement to a more focused, more intent quality.

"NAME_1," she said, "I'm going to ask you to do something that will require a bit more from you. Are you ready?"

He didn't know how to answer that question honestly, so he said, "Okay."

"I'm going to have NAME_5 apply some light restraints," she said, in the same easy, conversational tone she'd used for everything else tonight. "You're not going to resist this. You don't need to be worried about it. It's a demonstration of compliance under restraint — the degree to which post-hypnotic suggestion persists even when physical variables are changed."

He looked at NAME_5, who had moved to stand in front of him, the rope from earlier in her hands, and she gave him that small, warm, reassuring smile.

"I want to resist," he heard himself say.

NAME_4 stopped. It was a genuine stop — a pause that had a different quality from her theatrical pauses, a moment of actual consideration.

"Tell me more about that," she said.

"I want to resist," he said. "I'm choosing not to — or — you're choosing for me not to. But I want to. I want you to know that I want to."

There was a moment of quiet on the stage. Even the audience had stilled.

"I know," NAME_4 said, and something in her voice had changed slightly — a quality he hadn't heard from her before, something more considered. "That's important. That you can still identify what you want, even when you can't act on it." She looked at him for a moment. "Thank you for saying so."

Then she nodded at NAME_5, and NAME_5 moved forward with the rope, and he sat completely still in the chair while she worked.

---

NAME_5 was efficient and precise. This was clearly something she'd done many times — the way the rope moved through her hands had the quality of habitual skill, something practiced until it required no conscious attention. She worked from his wrists first, bringing them together behind the back of the chair and binding them in a configuration that was secure but not tight, not uncomfortable, nothing that dug into the skin or cut off circulation.

He was aware of his own stillness while this happened. He was aware of the completeness of it, the way not a single part of him moved to interfere — not a flinch, not a shift of weight, not even a change in his breathing. NAME_4 had done something in the last forty minutes that went beyond the original compulsion that had brought him here. She'd built on it, reinforced it, layered new instructions over the base structure so that he now sat in this chair with a quality of deep, settled stillness that felt nothing like calm.

It felt like a held breath.

NAME_5 moved to his ankles next, and he watched her work with a detachment that he recognized as artificial and still could not override. Two loops of rope, one at each ankle, securing each foot to a leg of the chair. Not tight. Functional.

She straightened up and stepped back, looking at him with a professional assessment that softened, just briefly, into something more personal.

"Okay?" she asked quietly.

He thought about the word. He thought about what okay meant under these specific circumstances. "I can feel it," he said, which wasn't an answer but was what came out.

She nodded as though she understood.

NAME_4 had been describing the process to the audience while NAME_5 worked, technical and articulate, her hands clasped behind her back in a posture that was somehow both relaxed and authoritative. Now she came to stand in front of him again, looking at him with that calculating, focused attention.

"How does the restraint affect the state?" she asked. "Be as specific as you can."

He thought about it. "It's —" he started, and stopped, and tried again. "It's like — when I couldn't close my hand before. Like there's a gap between what I want to do and what happens. But now the gap is physical. Before, it was just — internal."

"Externalized compliance," NAME_4 said to the audience, with the crisp satisfaction of someone identifying a concept they'd already defined. "The physical restraint provides a secondary layer of behavioral direction that interacts with the psychological compliance state. What we'll observe now is how the subject's responses shift when the compliance is anchored by both psychological and physical constraint simultaneously."

She turned back to him.

"NAME_1. I'm going to ask you some questions. I want you to answer honestly, as fully as you're able. The compliance state will support honest answers — it's difficult to give me something other than the truth right now, which you may find somewhat inconvenient. But the answers aren't going to leave this theater, and the audience has signed a confidentiality agreement. So let's be honest with each other."

He didn't know what she was going to ask. He had a vague, uncomfortable sense that it was going to be something personal, something he wouldn't ordinarily discuss in front of two hundred strangers, and he couldn't do anything about that sense except be aware of it.

"When you walked down the aisle toward the stage tonight," NAME_4 said, "and you understood that you couldn't stop yourself from doing it — what did you feel? Not what you thought. What you felt."

He sat with the question for a moment. "Scared," he said. "And —" He stopped.

"And?" she prompted.

"And something else," he said. "I don't know how to describe it."

"Try."

"Like —" he looked past her at the dark mass of the audience, which was very quiet, listening with an attentiveness that felt almost physical. "Like when you're on a roller coaster. Before the drop. When you know it's going to happen and you can't stop it and there's nothing to do but — be in it."

A quality of breath had changed in the theater. He felt it without quite understanding it.

"Fear and anticipation," NAME_4 said. "They use very similar neural pathways. They feel different from the outside but from the inside they're harder to distinguish than we'd like to believe." She looked at him with that focused expression. "When NAME_5 was applying the restraints, what were you thinking?"

"About the rope," he said.

"Specifically?"

"About how —" He stopped again. The honest answer was there in his mind, clear and complete, and the compliance state was doing its thing, smoothing the path between the thought and the voice. "About how it was very real. That this was really happening. That I was really sitting here and there was really rope on my wrists and it was real and not — not something I was choosing."

"Not something you were choosing," she said. "But something you were experiencing very fully."

"Yes."

"Is that still true?"

"Yes."

She nodded slowly. "The experience of genuine helplessness is different from the experience of performed helplessness," she said, addressing the audience but keeping her eyes on him. "On a stage, in a show, with a willing volunteer, even a convincingly compliant subject is choosing to comply at some level. There is always a background awareness that they could stop the experience if they truly wanted to. The safety net of agency. What you're seeing with NAME_1 tonight is the removal of that safety net — not permanently, not harmfully, but genuinely, in the moment. And what it produces is —" she paused. "What would you call it, NAME_1? What you're experiencing right now?"

He thought about it with more care than the question probably seemed to require.

"Honest," he said finally. "I think it's the most honest thing I've ever felt."

---

The response to this from the audience was not laughter. It was something quieter and more thoughtful, a collective settling, and NAME_4 looked at him for a moment with an expression he hadn't seen from her before tonight — not amusement, not calculation, not the smooth professionalism of a performer, but something that might have been genuine interest.

"That's perceptive," she said.

Then the performance mask went back on, smooth and seamless, and she turned to the audience and the demonstration continued.

---

What followed was, he would later think, the most methodical hour and a half he had ever experienced.

NAME_4 worked through him with the systematic thoroughness of someone completing a list — not cruelly, not carelessly, but with a precision that he found more disorienting than cruelty would have been. Cruelty would have given him something to push against. Precision just left him with nowhere to stand.

She demonstrated selective recall — giving him, and then taking from him, the memory of a specific detail, a color she'd asked him to fix in his mind ten minutes earlier, watching him search genuinely for something that was temporarily unavailable to him. She gave it back when she was done, and the sensation of the memory returning was like finding something in a pocket you'd already checked three times.

She demonstrated the sensory isolation — directing his attention away from specific inputs, and he'd sat there with the strange experience of knowing the lights were on but not quite being able to see the audience, knowing NAME_5 was speaking to him from his left but not quite being able to process the words, not because anything was wrong with his senses but because the information was simply not being forwarded.

She demonstrated something she called *anchored response* — pairing a physical gesture with a specific state, so that when she touched two fingers to the back of his hand a particular quality of settled calm flooded through him, instant and total, like a light switch. She demonstrated it four times, with the audience counting the seconds to response. He was consistent.

She demonstrated directed physical response — his left hand writing, slowly and carefully, a sentence he hadn't composed, while his right hand, when asked to write the same sentence simultaneously, produced nothing. The two hands worked independently, one directed, one his own.

Throughout all of this he sat in the chair with the rope on his wrists and ankles, not because he needed to — she had explained to the audience at one point that the restraints were not functionally necessary, given his compliance state — but because the physical dimension changed something about the quality of the demonstration, made visible something that was otherwise invisible.

*He cannot leave,* the restraints said. Even though he could not leave anyway.

He understood the theater of it. He understood it quite clearly. He just couldn't do anything about understanding it.

---

At some point during the second hour, NAME_5 brought him a glass of water without being asked, crouching beside the chair and holding it for him because his hands were bound, and he drank from it with a gratitude that surprised him with its intensity.

"Thank you," he said.

"Of course," she said, quiet and genuine.

She stayed beside him for a moment while NAME_4 consulted with someone at the edge of the stage — a stagehand, it looked like, something about a technical element for the next portion.

"You're doing well," NAME_5 said, and when he looked at her sharply she elaborated: "I mean that honestly, not as a performance thing. You're handling this better than most people do."

"Most people?" he said.

"The ones who come without choosing to," she said, and then seemed to consider whether she'd said too much, and then apparently decided she hadn't. "He's not the first," she said, with a slight gesture toward NAME_4. "She doesn't do this often. But when she does — you're handling it better."

"What happened to the others?" he asked.

NAME_5 was quiet for a moment. "They were fine," she said. "Afterward. That part is true."

He noted the specific shape of that answer. What it included and what it didn't.

"What does afterward look like?" he asked.

"The suggestion wears off," she said. "By morning, most of it is gone on its own. She'll clear the rest before you leave tonight — that's standard procedure. "And it's important that you know that I know. That I'm not missing or ignoring what you'd choose if you could choose right now."

The watch began to move.

He'd always thought the watch thing was a movie cliché, a theatrical shorthand that didn't actually work on real people in real life. He'd been fairly sure of this a moment ago.

He was less sure of it now.

The light in the theater seemed to simplify. Not darker, exactly — the lights hadn't changed — but less various, less complicated, as though the specific visual information of the room was condensing into its essential components. NAME_4's voice. The movement of the watch. The weight of the rope on his wrists.

"There's a point," NAME_4 was saying, in a voice that had changed its register slightly — not louder, not softer, but more contained, more directed, like a beam instead of a spread of light — "where the pathway becomes the destination. Where going further in isn't moving toward something, it's moving into something. You've been holding yourself at the edge of that tonight, NAME_1, and you've done that very well. But we're going to go now."

He wanted to say something. He had a sentence forming in his mind, specific words in a specific order.

He didn't say it.

Not because he couldn't. He thought he could have. The compliance state wasn't quite that total, not yet.

He didn't say it because some part of him, the part that had felt the roller coaster feeling, the part that had sat in this chair for two hours and experienced the strange, complete honesty of having no performance available to him, the part that had drunk water from NAME_5's hands and felt grateful — some part of him wanted to see what came next.

The ending came gradually.

She brought him back in the same methodical way she'd taken him further in, which he appreciated in retrospect — the reversal of the process rather than an abrupt cutoff, each layer of the state lifting in sequence, the room returning to its full, complex, slightly overwhelming reality in stages that his nervous system could accommodate.

He took a full breath.

Sixteen years old. NAME_1. Sat in a theater.

His hands were on his knees. He was wearing his good jeans and a clean shirt. He had taken three buses to get here. He had a phone in his pocket and his parents thought he was at Marcus's house.

He needed to text Marcus.

The thought of this practical, ordinary, embarrassingly teenage thing made him feel suddenly like himself in a way that nothing else had managed to accomplish for the past — he checked the large clock at the back of the theater — two and a half hours.

Two and a half hours.

---

After the audience filed out, chattering and animated, doing the thing audiences did where the experience they'd just had became a social event, a thing to discuss and share and carry home, NAME_1 remained in the chair because no one had told him to get up yet and he wasn't entirely sure his legs would do what he wanted if he tried.

NAME_5 sat on the stage beside the chair, not in a chair but simply on the boards, knees drawn up, apparently in no hurry.

"I will," she said. "In a moment. I want to make sure you're grounded enough first — it's better to do it when you're fully oriented."

I'll remove that cleanly tonight."

"After that, you leave here as yourself, with your own memories of tonight and no additional instructions I've left behind." She met his eyes. "You have my word on that."

He didn't know why he believed her. She had brought him here against his will, had held him on this stage for two and a half hours, had gone through the contents of his mind with the methodical thoroughness of a librarian cataloguing a collection, and had done all of this in front of an audience that had paid for the experience.

The clearing process was brief and quiet, without the theater of the evening's earlier work. NAME_4 sat in a chair she'd moved to face his, and NAME_5 sat to the side, and the two of them worked — if work was the right word for something that looked from the outside like a conversation, low-voiced and careful — through the structure that had been installed the previous week.

He felt it go. It was not dramatic. It was more like the feeling of a splinter being removed carefully — a small, contained discomfort, a brief awareness of something that had been present being absent, and then a settling.

"Done," NAME_4 said.

He sat with the absence for a moment. It was odd, the feeling of having had something removed that you hadn't known was there. Like a sound you'd stopped hearing because you'd heard it so long, and then it stopped and the silence was the loudest thing in the room.

"I have a question," he said.

"Ask it."

"Would you do it again? If I came to another show." He paused. "Not under compulsion. If I chose to come."

NAME_4 looked at him for a long moment. The expression on her face was complex and difficult to read, the most complex he'd seen from her all evening.

"That would be up to you," she said finally.

"But would you?"

"Yes," she said. "If you chose it. Freely."

He nodded slowly. He wasn't sure what to do with that answer. He wasn't sure what he was going to do with any of tonight, really, for quite some time. He suspected he was going to be thinking about it in fragments, in unexpected moments, for a long time after.

"Go home," NAME_5 said gently, and stood, and offered him her hand, and he took it and let her pull him to his feet.

His legs worked fine.

"NAME_1," NAME_4 said, from where she'd remained seated, watching him.

He turned.

"The quiet room," she said. "It's a considerable thing to have. Don't let it get noisy."

He wasn't entirely sure what she meant. He thought he might understand it better later.

"I won't," he said.

He walked off the stage and up the aisle and out into the night, where the street was wet from rain he hadn't heard while he was inside, the lights of the Vietnamese restaurant reflected in the puddles, a bus already visible at the end of the block.

He texted Marcus.

*Thanks for covering. Owe you.*

Marcus replied immediately. *was it worth it?*

He stood on the sidewalk for a moment, looking at the question.

*Yeah,* he typed. *Think so.*

He put his phone away and caught the bus, and the city moved past the windows, ordinary and enormous, and he sat with his hands on his knees and thought about the quiet room, and the roller coaster feeling, and the rope on his wrists, and NAME_5 holding a glass of water, and NAME_4's voice taking him further in.

By morning, she'd said, it would feel more like a memory and less like this.

He wasn't sure he wanted it to.

He caught his connection at the second stop and rode it to the end of his street and walked the last four blocks home under the clearing sky, and let himself in quietly, and went upstairs, and brushed his teeth, and lay down on his bed in the dark.

He was asleep in less than two minutes, and if he dreamed, he didn't remember it.

But in the morning, he remembered everything.

---

*End of Part 2*

"You see," NAME_2 addressed the audience with the easy confidence of a woman completely in control of her stage, her crowd, and the teenage girl standing rigidly beside her, "most volunteers require twenty, sometimes thirty minutes of careful induction work before we can really begin to have our fun. The conscious mind is a stubborn thing. It argues. It resists. It tells itself that none of this is real." She paused for effect, letting her eyes sweep the darkened rows of seats. "But NAME_1 here has been carrying a little gift I gave her for exactly one week. Haven't you, NAME_1?"

NAME_3 had moved to the side of the stage and was now wheeling out a tall, ornate chair — more of a throne, really, upholstered in deep red velvet, with curved armrests and a high back. "Let's get comfortable," NAME_2 said pleasantly, and NAME_3 guided NAME_1 toward the chair with a gentle but completely irresistible pressure at the small of her back.

She began to pace slowly across the stage, and her voice took on the quality of a lecture, though a decidedly entertaining one. She paused, glancing back at NAME_1 with what looked like genuine appreciation.

"There she is," NAME_2 said softly, and she was looking at NAME_1 with that same expression of genuine appreciation, and NAME_1 realized that her own face had changed somehow, that the tight, defensive set of it had smoothed out. "Both of you."

The pendant moved. Not dramatically, not swinging in wide arcs the way you saw in movies — just a slow, deliberate rotation, catching the light in small, regular intervals. NAME_1 watched it without quite deciding to.

"The conscious mind," NAME_2 said, her voice still in that rhythm, "is very busy. It has so much to do. So many things to track, to analyze, to worry about. So many narratives to maintain." The pendant turned. Light, shadow, light, shadow. "It works so hard. All the time. Every day." A pause. "It must be tired."

NAME_1 thought: *I'm not tired, I'm —*

She lost the end of the sentence.

This had never happened to her before. She was a verbally precise person, someone who finished sentences, who chose words with care, who held the thread of her own thoughts with practiced competence. And the end of the sentence was simply not there. She reached for it and found warm, smooth blankness, like putting her hand out in the dark and finding not an edge but a gentle, padded wall.

"That's right," said NAME_2, from somewhere that felt like it might be inside NAME_1's own head. "You don't have to hold onto it. It's all right to let it go for a while."

*Let what go,* NAME_1 thought, and this thought too trailed off into warmth before it arrived anywhere.

The pendant turned. Light, shadow, light.

# The Orphanage at Nightfall

The week has been going wonderfully. The kids at Meadowbrook Orphanage adore you — you've been playing tag in the yard, reading stories after dinner, helping with homework. You've earned the trust of nearly every child here.

Nearly.

Lily has watched you all week with those sharp green eyes, arms crossed, never quite joining the games. When you tried to include her, she just smirked like she knew something you didn't.

You should have paid more attention to that smirk.

---

It's past midnight when it happens.

You're deep asleep when a soft giggling pulls you toward consciousness. You blink, disoriented, and see Lily standing at the foot of your bed, her dark hair loose around her shoulders, both palms glowing with a faint amber light.

"Lily?" you say, voice still thick with sleep. "What are you — how did you get in here?"

"Shh," she whispers cheerfully. "This'll only take a second, Rai."

Before you can sit up, the amber light surges forward.

It hits you like a warm wave, spreading from your chest outward to every fingertip. You try to speak and only manage a startled sound. The feeling isn't painful — that's almost the strangest part. It's soft, almost like sinking into bathwater, and it pulls at something deep inside you.

Your hands are the first thing you notice. You watch them as the fingers shorten, as the knuckles round out, as the faint veins that have only recently become visible beneath your skin simply *fade*. Your hands become small and smooth, the hands of someone who has never once had to worry about anything serious.

Then it moves upward through your arms. The lean muscle you've built up over years of training softens and diminishes, your biceps shrinking down, your shoulders narrowing inward like a shirt collar slowly being drawn closed.

You try to stand and immediately stumble — your legs are shorter now, your center of gravity all wrong. You grab the bedframe and your fingers barely wrap around it. You're *small.* The mattress that felt normal-sized an hour ago now feels enormous beneath you.

Your vision shifts as your perspective drops another few inches. The ceiling feels further away. The room feels bigger. Lily, who is ten years old, is now looking at you almost *eye to eye.*

Your throat tightens — and then your voice comes out wrong. You say "stop" and it comes out high and reedy and young, the voice of a child who is maybe seven, maybe eight years old at most.

You look down at yourself. Pajamas that fit you an hour ago are now a tent draped over a tiny frame.

Lily puts a fist to her mouth to stifle her laughter.

"There," she announces, examining her work with enormous satisfaction. "Now you're *one of us.*"

You stare up at her, small hands balling into fists.

"Lily." Your tiny voice trembles with indignation. "Change me *back.*"

She tilts her head, grinning wickedly.

"Hmm. No."

text: introduce NSGA-III to me in detail
answer:
# NSGA-III: Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III

## Overview

NSGA-III is a **many-objective evolutionary optimization algorithm** proposed by **Deb and Jain (2014)** as an extension of NSGA-II. While NSGA-II works well for 2-3 objective problems, it struggles with **many-objective problems (4+ objectives)** due to the breakdown of dominance-based selection pressure. NSGA-III addresses this by replacing the crowding distance mechanism with a **reference point-based diversity preservation** strategy.

> **Key Paper:** Deb, K., & Jain, H. (2014). *An Evolutionary Many-Objective Optimization Algorithm Using Reference-Point-Based Nondominated Sorting Approach, Part I: Solving Problems With Box Constraints.* IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation, 18(4), 577–601.

---

## Motivation: Why NSGA-II Fails for Many Objectives

| Problem | NSGA-II Behavior |
|---|---|
| 2–3 objectives | Works well |
| 4+ objectives | Nearly all solutions become non-dominated → no selection pressure |
| Diversity | Crowding distance fails in high dimensions |
| Convergence | Slows dramatically |

When the number of objectives increases, the probability that any two solutions dominate each other decreases exponentially. The Pareto front concept loses discriminative power.

---

## Core Concepts

### 1. Reference Points (Structured Diversity)

The central innovation of NSGA-III is the use of **pre-defined reference points** on a **normalized hyperplane** to guide population diversity.

#### Das-Dennis Reference Point Generation
Reference points are systematically placed on a **unit simplex** (hyperplane where all objective values sum to 1):

$$\sum_{i=1}^{M} f_i = 1, \quad f_i \geq 0$$

The number of reference points $H$ for $M$ objectives with $p$ divisions per axis:

$$H = \binom{M + p - 1}{p}$$

**Example:**
| Objectives (M) | Divisions (p) | Reference Points (H) |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 | 15 |
| 5 | 6 | 210 |
| 8 | 3 | 120 |
| 10 | 3 | 220 |

For many objectives, a **two-layer reference point** approach is used (inner + outer layers) to avoid too many or too few points.

```
M=3, p=4 simplex visualization:

        f1
        /\
       /  \
      / .. \
     / .  . \
    /________\
  f3          f2

  Each dot = one reference point
```

---

### 2. Objective Space Normalization

Before associating solutions with reference points, objectives are **normalized** to [0, 1]:

#### Step-by-step:
1. **Find ideal point** $z^{min}_i = \min f_i$ over current population
2. **Translate** objectives: $f'_i = f_i - z^{min}_i$
3. **Find extreme points** (using ASF - Achievement Scalarizing Function)
4. **Construct hyperplane** through extreme points
5. **Normalize** using intercepts $a_i$:

$$\bar{f}_i = \frac{f'_i}{a_i}$$

The **Achievement Scalarizing Function (ASF)**:
$$\text{ASF}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \max_{i=1}^{M} \frac{f'_i(\mathbf{x})}{w_i}$$

Used to find extreme solutions (set $w_i = 1$ for target axis, $w_j = 10^{-6}$ for others).

---

### 3. Association: Linking Solutions to Reference Points

Each solution is associated with the **nearest reference point** using **perpendicular distance**:

#### Process:
1. Draw a **reference line** from origin through each reference point
2. For each solution, compute **perpendicular distance** to each reference line
3. Assign solution to the reference line with **minimum distance**

```
Normalized hyperplane

Ref line ───────→ • Reference Point
                 ↑ perpendicular
      Solution • ┘ distance d⊥
```

**Perpendicular distance** from point $\mathbf{s}$ to line through $\mathbf{r}$:

$$d(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}) = \left\| \mathbf{s} - \frac{\mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}|^2} \mathbf{r} \right\|$$

---

### 4. Niche Count

The **niche count** $\rho_j$ of reference point $j$ = number of population members associated with it.

- Low niche count → **underrepresented region** → preferred for selection
- High niche count → **crowded region** → less preferred

---

## Full Algorithm Walkthrough

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              NSGA-III Main Loop                      │
│                                                     │
│  Initialize population P (size N)                   │
│  Generate reference points Z                        │
│                                                     │
│  Repeat until termination:                          │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ 1. Create offspring Q via                     │  │
│  │    - Tournament selection                     │  │
│  │    - Crossover (SBX)                          │  │
│  │    - Mutation (polynomial)                    │  │
│  │                                               │  │
│  │ 2. Combine: R = P ∪ Q  (size 2N)             │  │
│  │                                               │  │
│  │ 3. Non-dominated Sorting of R                 │  │
│  │    → Fronts F1, F2, F3, ...                   │  │
│  │                                               │  │
│  │ 4. Build new population P':                   │  │
│  │    Add fronts until |P'| ≥ N                  │  │
│  │    Last accepted front = Fl                   │  │
│  │                                               │  │
│  │ 5. If |P'| == N → done                        │  │
│  │    Else → Niching procedure                   │  │
│  │    (select from Fl to fill P to size N)       │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## The Niching Procedure (Key Step)

This is what **distinguishes NSGA-III from NSGA-II**.

When the last front $F_l$ cannot be fully included (would exceed $N$), we need to **selectively pick** $K = N - |P' \setminus F_l|$ solutions from $F_l$.

```
Procedure Niching(K, Jr, Zr, P_next, Fl):
  
  WHILE |chosen| < K:
    
    1. Find reference point j* with minimum niche count ρ_j
       among reference points in Jr
       (break ties randomly)
    
    2. Among solutions in Fl associated with j*:
    
       CASE A: ρ_j* == 0 (no member yet from P_next)
           → Pick solution with MINIMUM perpendicular
             distance to reference line j*
       
       CASE B: ρ_j* > 0 (already has members)
           → Pick a RANDOM solution from Fl
             associated with j*
    
    3. Add chosen solution to P_next
       Increment ρ_j*
       Remove solution from Fl
    
    4. If no solution in Fl associated with j*:
           Remove j* from Jr
```

**Rationale:**
- Prefer filling **empty niches** first (Case A → pick closest for precision)
- For already-filled niches, **random selection** to avoid bias (Case B)

---

## Algorithm Pseudocode

```python
Algorithm NSGA-III:

Input:  N (population size), Z (reference points), 
        max_gen (generations)
Output: Final Pareto front approximation

# Initialization
P = initialize_population(N)
evaluate(P)
Z = generate_reference_points(M, p)

for gen = 1 to max_gen:
    
    # Reproduction
    Q = make_offspring(P)   # selection + SBX + mutation
    evaluate(Q)
    
    # Combination
    R = P ∪ Q
    
    # Non-dominated Sorting
    [F1, F2, ..., Fk] = non_dominated_sort(R)
    
    # Build next generation
    P_next = []
    i = 1
    while |P_next| + |Fi| <= N:
        P_next = P_next ∪ Fi
        i += 1
    Fl = Fi  # last front
    
    # Normalize objectives
    normalize(P_next ∪ Fl)
    
    # Associate solutions with reference points
    associate(P_next ∪ Fl, Z)
    
    # Compute niche counts for P_next
    ρ = compute_niche_counts(P_next, Z)
    
    # Niching selection from Fl
    K = N - |P_next|
    P_next = niching(K, Z, ρ, P_next, Fl)
    
    P = P_next

return P
```

---

## Genetic Operators Used

### Simulated Binary Crossover (SBX)
- Creates offspring with spread similar to parents
- Controlled by distribution index $\eta_c$ (typically 30)

### Polynomial Mutation
- Small perturbations around parent
- Controlled by $\eta_m$ (typically 20)
- Mutation probability: $p_m = 1/n$ ($n$ = number of variables)

### Tournament Selection (for NSGA-III)
- Uses **random selection** or front-rank-based selection
- Unlike NSGA-II, crowding distance is NOT used in tournament

---

## Complexity Analysis

| Component | Complexity |
|---|---|
| Non-dominated sorting | $O(MN^2)$ |
| Normalization | $O(MN)$ |
| Association | $O(MNH)$ |
| Niching | $O(NH)$ |
| **Total per generation** | **$O(MN^2)$** |

Where $M$ = objectives, $N$ = population size, $H$ = reference points

---

## NSGA-III vs NSGA-II Comparison

| Feature | NSGA-II | NSGA-III |
|---|---|---|
| Year | 2002 | 2014 |
| Diversity mechanism | Crowding distance | Reference points |
| Suitable for | 2–3 objectives | 3–15+ objectives |
| Hyperplane normalization | No | Yes |
| User-defined structure | No | Yes (reference points) |
| Selection in last front | Best crowding distance | Niching procedure |
| Computational overhead | Low | Moderate |

---

## Visual Intuition

```
2D Pareto Front (NSGA-II works fine):

f2 ↑
   |  * * 
   |    * *
   |      * *
   └──────────→ f1
   Crowding distance OK here

5D Many-Objective (NSGA-III needed):

  All solutions appear 
  non-dominated →        Reference points spread
  no pressure!           solutions uniformly:
  
  ?? ?? ?? ?? ??    vs   •  •  •  •  •
  ?? ?? ?? ?? ??         •  •  •  •  •
  ?? ?? ?? ?? ??         •  •  •  •  •
```

---

## Variants and Extensions

| Variant | Description |
|---|---|
| **NSGA-III Part II** (Jain & Deb, 2014) | Handles constraints, user preferences |
| **U-NSGA-III** | Unified version, better for 2-3 objectives too |
| **A-NSGA-III** | Adaptive reference points |
| **ANSGA-III** | With archive for unbounded population |
| **C-NSGA-III** | Constrained version |
| **θ-DEA** | Reference point + angle-based dominance |

---

## Parameter Settings (Practical Guide)

| Parameter | Recommended Value |
|---|---|
| Population size N | ≥ H (match reference points) |
| SBX index $\eta_c$ | 30 |
| Mutation index $\eta_m$ | 20 |
| Crossover probability | 1.0 |
| Mutation probability | 1/n |
| Divisions p (outer) | Depends on M |
| Generations | 300–1000+ |

**Suggested divisions for M objectives:**

| M | p (single layer) | p1, p2 (two layers) |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 12 | — |
| 5 | 6 | — |
| 8 | 3 | (3, 2) |
| 10 | 3 | (3, 2) |
| 15 | 2 | (2, 1) |

---

## Test Problems

NSGA-III is typically benchmarked on:

| Suite | Problems | Objectives |
|---|---|---|
| **DTLZ** | DTLZ1–7 | 3, 5, 8, 10, 15 |
| **WFG** | WFG1–9 | 3–10 |
| **ZDT** | ZDT1–6 | 2–3 |
| **MaF** | MaF1–15 | 3–15 |

---

## Strengths and Limitations

### ✅ Strengths
- Excellent for **4–15 objective** problems
- Well-distributed solutions via reference points
- Structured diversity without distance computation
- Theoretically sound convergence
- Widely implemented (PlatEMO, pymoo, DEAP, jMetal)

### ❌ Limitations
- Reference points must be **pre-defined** (domain knowledge needed)
- Performance depends on **Pareto front shape** matching reference hyperplane
- Struggles with **degenerate** or **disconnected** fronts
- More parameters to tune than NSGA-II
- High-dimensional variable spaces still challenging

---

## Implementation (Python with pymoo)

```python
from pymoo.algorithms.moo.nsga3 import NSGA3
from pymoo.util.ref_dirs import get_reference_directions
from pymoo.problems import get_problem
from pymoo.optimize import minimize

# Define reference directions (reference points)
ref_dirs = get_reference_directions(
    "das-dennis",     # Das-Dennis method
    n_dim=3,          # number of objectives
    n_partitions=12   # divisions
)

# Setup algorithm
algorithm = NSGA3(
    ref_dirs=ref_dirs,
    pop_size=92        # should match or exceed H
)

# Define problem (e.g., DTLZ1 with 3 objectives)
problem = get_problem("dtlz1", n_obj=3)

# Run optimization
result = minimize(
    problem,
    algorithm,
    termination=('n_gen', 300),
    seed=42,
    verbose=True
)

print("Pareto front shape:", result.F.shape)
```

---

## Summary

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   NSGA-III Summary                    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Goal:      Many-objective optimization (4-15+ obj)  │
│  Key idea:  Reference point-based diversity          │
│  Steps:     1. Non-dominated sorting (like NSGA-II)  │
│             2. Normalize objective space             │
│             3. Associate solutions → ref points      │
│             4. Niche-preserving selection            │
│  Strength:  Uniform coverage of Pareto front         │
│  Weakness:  Fixed reference points, front shape      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

NSGA-III represents a **significant leap** in evolutionary many-objective optimization by shifting the diversity mechanism from distance-based to **structure-based** (reference points), making it one of the most widely used and cited algorithms in the field.

text: NAME_1! Teach me about codeql
answer:
# CodeQL - A Comprehensive Guide 🔍

## What is CodeQL?

**CodeQL** is a **semantic code analysis engine** developed by GitHub (acquired from Semmle). It treats code **like data** — you can write queries to find bugs, vulnerabilities, and patterns across your codebase.

> Think of it as **"SQL for source code"**

---

## Core Concepts

### 1. 📦 Databases
CodeQL first **extracts** your source code into a **relational database**
```
Source Code → CodeQL Extractor → CodeQL Database
```
- Contains facts about the code (AST, data flow, control flow)
- Language-specific extractors exist

### 2. 🔎 Queries (.ql files)
You write queries to find patterns in the database
```ql
-- Find hardcoded passwords (simple example)
import java

from StringLiteral s
where s.getValue().toLowerCase().matches("%password%")
select s, "Possible hardcoded password"
```

### 3. 📚 Libraries
- Pre-built modules for common patterns
- Data flow, taint tracking, control flow helpers

---

## Supported Languages

| Language | Support Level |
|----------|--------------|
| C/C++ | ✅ Full |
| Java/Kotlin | ✅ Full |
| Python | ✅ Full |
| JavaScript/TypeScript | ✅ Full |
| C# | ✅ Full |
| Go | ✅ Full |
| Ruby | ✅ Full |
| Swift | 🔄 Beta |

---

## Key Features

### 🌊 Taint Tracking
Track **untrusted data** flowing through your program
```ql
import java
import semmle.code.java.dataflow.TaintTracking

class SqlInjectionConfig extends TaintTracking::Configuration {
  SqlInjectionConfig() { this = "SqlInjectionConfig" }

  override predicate isSource(DataFlow::Node source) {
    source instanceof RemoteFlowSource
  }

  override predicate isSink(DataFlow::Node sink) {
    sink instanceof SqlQuerySink
  }
}
```

### 🔄 Data Flow Analysis
- **Local** data flow (within a function)
- **Global** data flow (across functions/files)

### 🌳 AST Analysis
Query the **Abstract Syntax Tree** directly
```ql
import python

from FunctionDef f
where f.getName() = "eval"
select f, "Found eval function"
```

---

## Getting Started

### Step 1 - Install CLI
```bash
# Download from GitHub releases
# https://github.com/github/codeql-cli-binaries

# Verify installation
codeql version
```

### Step 2 - Create a Database
```bash
# For Java project
codeql database create my-db \
  --language=java \
  --command="mvn clean install"

# For Python project
codeql database create my-db \
  --language=python

# For JavaScript
codeql database create my-db \
  --language=javascript
```

### Step 3 - Run a Query
```bash
# Run a single query
codeql query run my-query.ql \
  --database=my-db

# Run a query suite
codeql database analyze my-db \
  --format=sarif-latest \
  --output=results.sarif
```

---

## Query Structure

```ql
/**
 * @name Query Name
 * @description What this query finds
 * @kind problem
 * @severity error
 * @tags security
 */

import java  // Import language library

// Define predicates (reusable logic)
predicate isUserInput(Expr e) {
  e instanceof MethodAccess and
  e.(MethodAccess).getMethod().getName() = "getParameter"
}

// Main query
from MethodAccess call, Expr arg
where 
  call.getMethod().getName() = "executeQuery" and
  arg = call.getAnArgument() and
  isUserInput(arg)
select call, "Potential SQL injection"
```

Define una arquitectura como código en una implementación realizada en NAME_1
answer:
# Arquitectura como Código en Terraform

## ¿Qué es Arquitectura como Código?

La **Arquitectura como Código (AaC)** es la práctica de definir, documentar y gestionar la infraestructura y arquitectura de sistemas mediante archivos de código versionables y reproducibles.

---

## Implementación en Terraform

### Estructura del Proyecto

```
arquitectura-proyecto/
├── main.tf
├── variables.tf
├── outputs.tf
├── terraform.tfvars
├── modules/
│   ├── networking/
│   │   ├── main.tf
│   │   ├── variables.tf
│   │   └── outputs.tf
│   ├── compute/
│   │   ├── main.tf
│   │   ├── variables.tf
│   │   └── outputs.tf
│   └── database/
│       ├── main.tf
│       ├── variables.tf
│       └── outputs.tf
└── environments/
    ├── dev.tfvars
    ├── staging.tfvars
    └── prod.tfvars
```

---

### Archivo Principal `main.tf`

```hcl
# ============================================
# ARQUITECTURA COMO CÓDIGO - AWS con Terraform
# ============================================

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"
  
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }

  # Backend remoto para estado compartido
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "mi-terraform-state-bucket"
    key            = "arquitectura/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    encrypt        = true
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-lock-table"
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
  
  default_tags {
    tags = {
      Proyecto     = var.proyecto
      Ambiente     = var.ambiente
      GestionadoPor = "Terraform"
      Equipo       = var.equipo
    }
  }
}

# ============================================
# MÓDULO DE RED (VPC)
# ============================================
module "networking" {
  source = "./modules/networking"

  proyecto        = var.proyecto
  ambiente        = var.ambiente
  vpc_cidr        = var.vpc_cidr
  azs             = var.availability_zones
  subnets_publicas  = var.subnets_publicas_cidr
  subnets_privadas  = var.subnets_privadas_cidr
  enable_nat_gateway = var.enable_nat_gateway
}

# ============================================
# MÓDULO DE CÓMPUTO (EC2 / ECS)
# ============================================
module "compute" {
  source = "./modules/compute"

  proyecto         = var.proyecto
  ambiente         = var.ambiente
  vpc_id           = module.networking.vpc_id
  subnet_privada_ids = module.networking.subnet_privada_ids
  subnet_publica_ids = module.networking.subnet_publica_ids
  instancia_tipo   = var.instancia_tipo
  min_instancias   = var.min_instancias
  max_instancias   = var.max_instancias
  ami_id           = var.ami_id
}

# ============================================
# MÓDULO DE BASE DE DATOS (RDS)
# ============================================
module "database" {
  source = "./modules/database"

  proyecto           = var.proyecto
  ambiente           = var.ambiente
  vpc_id             = module.networking.vpc_id
  subnet_privada_ids = module.networking.subnet_privada_ids
  db_engine          = var.db_engine
  db_version         = var.db_version
  db_instance_class  = var.db_instance_class
  db_nombre          = var.db_nombre
  db_usuario         = var.db_usuario
  db_password        = var.db_password
  multi_az           = var.ambiente == "prod" ? true : false
  sg_compute_id      = module.compute.security_group_id
}
```

---

### Módulo de Red `modules/networking/main.tf`

```hcl
# ============================================
# VPC PRINCIPAL
# ============================================
resource "aws_vpc" "principal" {
  cidr_block           = var.vpc_cidr
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
  enable_dns_support   = true

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-vpc"
  }
}

# ============================================
# SUBNETS PÚBLICAS
# ============================================
resource "aws_subnet" "publica" {
  count             = length(var.subnets_publicas)
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.principal.id
  cidr_block        = var.subnets_publicas[count.index]
  availability_zone = var.azs[count.index]
  
  map_public_ip_on_launch = true

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-subnet-publica-${count.index + 1}"
    Tipo = "Publica"
  }
}

# ============================================
# SUBNETS PRIVADAS
# ============================================
resource "aws_subnet" "privada" {
  count             = length(var.subnets_privadas)
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.principal.id
  cidr_block        = var.subnets_privadas[count.index]
  availability_zone = var.azs[count.index]

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-subnet-privada-${count.index + 1}"
    Tipo = "Privada"
  }
}

# ============================================
# INTERNET GATEWAY
# ============================================
resource "aws_internet_gateway" "igw" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.principal.id

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-igw"
  }
}

# ============================================
# NAT GATEWAY (para subnets privadas)
# ============================================
resource "aws_eip" "nat" {
  count  = var.enable_nat_gateway ? length(var.subnets_publicas) : 0
  domain = "vpc"

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-eip-${count.index + 1}"
  }
}

resource "aws_nat_gateway" "nat" {
  count         = var.enable_nat_gateway ? length(var.subnets_publicas) : 0
  allocation_id = aws_eip.nat[count.index].id
  subnet_id     = aws_subnet.publica[count.index].id

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-nat-${count.index + 1}"
  }

  depends_on = [aws_internet_gateway.igw]
}

# ============================================
# TABLAS DE RUTAS
# ============================================
resource "aws_route_table" "publica" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.principal.id

  route {
    cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
    gateway_id = aws_internet_gateway.igw.id
  }

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-rt-publica"
  }
}

resource "aws_route_table" "privada" {
  count  = var.enable_nat_gateway ? length(var.subnets_privadas) : 0
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.principal.id

  route {
    cidr_block     = "0.0.0.0/0"
    nat_gateway_id = aws_nat_gateway.nat[count.index].id
  }

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-rt-privada-${count.index + 1}"
  }
}

# Asociaciones de tablas de rutas
resource "aws_route_table_association" "publica" {
  count          = length(aws_subnet.publica)
  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.publica[count.index].id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.publica.id
}

resource "aws_route_table_association" "privada" {
  count          = length(aws_subnet.privada)
  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.privada[count.index].id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.privada[count.index].id
}
```

---

### Módulo de Cómputo `modules/compute/main.tf`

```hcl
# ============================================
# SECURITY GROUP - LOAD BALANCER
# ============================================
resource "aws_security_group" "alb" {
  name        = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-sg-alb"
  description = "Security Group para Application Load Balancer"
  vpc_id      = var.vpc_id

  ingress {
    description = "HTTP desde Internet"
    from_port   = 80
    to_port     = 80
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }

  ingress {
    description = "HTTPS desde Internet"
    from_port   = 443
    to_port     = 443
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }

  egress {
    from_port   = 0
    to_port     = 0
    protocol    = "-1"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-sg-alb"
  }
}

# ============================================
# SECURITY GROUP - APLICACIÓN
# ============================================
resource "aws_security_group" "app" {
  name        = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-sg-app"
  description = "Security Group para instancias de aplicación"
  vpc_id      = var.vpc_id

  ingress {
    description     = "Tráfico desde ALB"
    from_port       = 8080
    to_port         = 8080
    protocol        = "tcp"
    security_groups = [aws_security_group.alb.id]
  }

  egress {
    from_port   = 0
    to_port     = 0
    protocol    = "-1"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-sg-app"
  }
}

# ============================================
# APPLICATION LOAD BALANCER
# ============================================
resource "aws_lb" "principal" {
  name               = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-alb"
  internal           = false
  load_balancer_type = "application"
  security_groups    = [aws_security_group.alb.id]
  subnets            = var.subnet_publica_ids

  enable_deletion_protection = var.ambiente == "prod" ? true : false

  tags = {
    Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-alb"
  }
}

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "app" {
  name     = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-tg"
  port     = 8080
  protocol = "HTTP"
  vpc_id   = var.vpc_id

  health_check {
    enabled             = true
    healthy_threshold   = 2
    unhealthy_threshold = 2
    timeout             = 5
    interval            = 30
    path                = "/health"
    matcher             = "200"
  }
}

resource "aws_lb_listener" "http" {
  load_balancer_arn = aws_lb.principal.arn
  port              = "80"
  protocol          = "HTTP"

  default_action {
    type             = "forward"
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.app.arn
  }
}

# ============================================
# AUTO SCALING GROUP
# ============================================
resource "aws_launch_template" "app" {
  name_prefix   = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-lt-"
  image_id      = var.ami_id
  instance_type = var.instancia_tipo

  network_interfaces {
    associate_public_ip_address = false
    security_groups             = [aws_security_group.app.id]
  }

  user_data = base64encode(<<-EOF
    #!/bin/bash
    yum update -y
    yum install -y docker
    systemctl start docker
    systemctl enable docker
  EOF
  )

  tag_specifications {
    resource_type = "instance"
    tags = {
      Name = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-instancia"
    }
  }

  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true
  }
}

resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "app" {
  name                = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-asg"
  vpc_zone_identifier = var.subnet_privada_ids
  target_group_arns   = [aws_lb_target_group.app.arn]
  health_check_type   = "ELB"
  
  min_size         = var.min_instancias
  max_size         = var.max_instancias
  desired_capacity = var.min_instancias

  launch_template {
    id      = aws_launch_template.app.id
    version = "$Latest"
  }

  tag {
    key                 = "Name"
    value               = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-asg"
    propagate_at_launch = true
  }
}

# Política de escalado automático
resource "aws_autoscaling_policy" "cpu_alto" {
  name                   = "${var.proyecto}-${var.ambiente}-scale-up"
  autoscaling_group_name = aws_autoscaling_group.app.name
  adjustment_type        = "ChangeInCapacity"
  scaling_adjustment     = 1
  cooldown               = 300
}
```

---

I think you're asking about **Makefile + Ansible** (NAME_1 likely got filtered). Here's how to combine them:

---

## Why Use Makefile with Ansible?

- Simplify long `ansible-playbook` commands
- Standardize common operations
- Provide shortcuts for teams
- Chain multiple operations together

---

## Basic Example

```makefile
# Makefile

INVENTORY = inventory/hosts
PLAYBOOK_DIR = playbooks
VAULT_FILE = vault/secrets.yml

# Default target
.DEFAULT_GOAL := help

.PHONY: help deploy ping setup

help:
	@echo "Available targets:"
	@echo "  ping     - Test connectivity"
	@echo "  setup    - Run setup playbook"
	@echo "  deploy   - Deploy application"

ping:
	ansible all -i $(INVENTORY) -m ping

setup:
	ansible-playbook -i $(INVENTORY) $(PLAYBOOK_DIR)/setup.yml

deploy:
	ansible-playbook -i $(INVENTORY) $(PLAYBOOK_DIR)/deploy.yml

vault-edit:
	ansible-vault edit $(VAULT_FILE)
```

---

## Advanced Example

```makefile
# Makefile

ENV ?= staging
INVENTORY = inventory/$(ENV)
TAGS ?= ""
LIMIT ?= ""
VERBOSE ?= ""

# Build flags dynamically
FLAGS =
ifneq ($(TAGS), "")
    FLAGS += --tags $(TAGS)
endif
ifneq ($(LIMIT), "")
    FLAGS += --limit $(LIMIT)
endif
ifneq ($(VERBOSE), "")
    FLAGS += -$(VERBOSE)
endif

.PHONY: deploy rollback check lint

deploy:
	ansible-playbook -i $(INVENTORY) playbooks/deploy.yml $(FLAGS)

rollback:
	ansible-playbook -i $(INVENTORY) playbooks/rollback.yml $(FLAGS)

# Dry run
check:
	ansible-playbook -i $(INVENTORY) playbooks/deploy.yml --check $(FLAGS)

# Lint playbooks
lint:
	ansible-lint playbooks/*.yml

# Install requirements
requirements:
	ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml
```

---

## Usage Examples

```bash
# Simple commands
make ping
make deploy
make setup

# With variables
make deploy ENV=production
make deploy TAGS=nginx
make deploy LIMIT=webservers VERBOSE=vv

# Dry run
make check ENV=staging
```

---

## With Docker/CI Pipeline

```makefile
DOCKER_IMAGE = ansible:latest

ansible-run:
	docker run --rm \
		-v $(PWD):/ansible \
		-v ~/.ssh:/root/.ssh \
		$(DOCKER_IMAGE) \
		ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts playbooks/site.yml

ci-deploy:
	@echo "Running in CI mode..."
	ansible-playbook \
		-i inventory/$(ENV) \
		--vault-password-file .vault_pass \
		playbooks/deploy.yml
```

---

## Tips

| Tip | Description |
|-----|-------------|
| `.PHONY` | Always declare non-file targets |
| `?=` | Allow variable overrides from CLI |
| `@` prefix | Suppress command echo |
| `help` target | Self-documenting Makefile |

# Triggering Another Pipeline from a Pipeline in Azure DevOps

## Overview
Here are the main ways to trigger another pipeline from within a pipeline:

---

## Method 1: Using `resources` + Pipeline Trigger (Automatic)

```yaml
# Pipeline B (downstream pipeline)
resources:
  pipelines:
    - pipeline: upstream-pipeline    # Alias
      source: 'Pipeline-A-Name'      # Exact name of Pipeline A
      trigger: true                  # Auto-trigger when Pipeline A completes
```

---

## Method 2: Using REST API Task (Manual Trigger)

```yaml
# Pipeline A - triggers Pipeline B manually
steps:
  - task: PowerShell@2
    displayName: 'Trigger Another Pipeline'
    inputs:
      targetType: 'inline'
      script: |
        $organization = "YourOrg"
        $project      = "YourProject"
        $pipelineId   = 123          # ID of Pipeline B
        $token        = "$(System.AccessToken)"
        
        $base64Token = [Convert]::ToBase64String(
          [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes(":$token")
        )
        
        $headers = @{
          Authorization  = "Basic $base64Token"
          "Content-Type" = "application/json"
        }
        
        $body = @{
          resources = @{
            repositories = @{
              self = @{
                refName = "refs/heads/main"
              }
            }
          }
        } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10
        
        $uri = "https://dev.azure.com/$organization/$project/_apis/pipelines/$pipelineId/runs?api-version=7.0"
        
        Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $uri -Method POST -Headers $headers -Body $body
    env:
      SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN: $(System.AccessToken)
```

---

## Method 3: Using `azure-devops` CLI Task

```yaml
steps:
  - task: AzureCLI@2
    displayName: 'Trigger Pipeline via CLI'
    inputs:
      azureSubscription: 'YourServiceConnection'
      scriptType: 'bash'
      scriptLocation: 'inlineScript'
      inlineScript: |
        az pipelines run \
          --organization "https://dev.azure.com/YourOrg" \
          --project "YourProject" \
          --id 123 \
          --branch "main"
```

---

## Method 4: Template Reference (Reusable Steps)

```yaml
# main-pipeline.yaml
steps:
  - template: templates/deploy-steps.yaml   # Reference shared template
    parameters:
      environment: 'production'
      region: 'eastus'
```

```yaml
# templates/deploy-steps.yaml
parameters:
  - name: environment
    type: string
  - name: region
    type: string

steps:
  - script: echo "Deploying to ${{ parameters.environment }}"
    displayName: 'Deploy Step'
    
  - script: echo "Region: ${{ parameters.region }}"
    displayName: 'Show Region'
```

---

## Method 5: Stages Dependency Trigger

```yaml
stages:
  - stage: Build
    jobs:
      - job: BuildJob
        steps:
          - script: echo "Building..."

  - stage: TriggerDownstream
    dependsOn: Build               # Runs after Build stage
    condition: succeeded()
    jobs:
      - job: TriggerJob
        steps:
          - task: PowerShell@2
            inputs:
              targetType: 'inline'
              script: |
                # REST API call to trigger another pipeline
                Write-Host "Triggering downstream pipeline..."
```

---

## ✅ Comparison Table

| Method | Use Case | Complexity |
|--------|----------|------------|
| `resources` trigger | Auto chain pipelines | Low |
| REST API Task | Full control & parameters | Medium |
| Azure CLI Task | Simple trigger with CLI | Medium |
| Template Reference | Reuse steps/jobs | Low |
| Stage Dependency | Sequential stage control | Low |

---

## 🔑 Required Permissions

```yaml
# Add this to allow pipeline to trigger others
pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'

# In Project Settings > Pipelines > Settings:
# ✅ Enable: "Allow scripts to access the OAuth token"

variables:
  - name: SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN
    value: $(System.AccessToken)
```

> **Tip:** Make sure the pipeline service account has **"Queue builds"** permission on the target pipeline.

```dockerfile
FROM debian:11-slim

RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \

    apt-get clean && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app
```
